item.title: #505 《GTA 6》、犯罪、珠宝抢劫、监狱、腐败警察、黑手党、迈阿密与金钱
item.description: 拉里·劳顿结合自身经历谈《GTA 6》与现实犯罪、珠宝抢劫、监狱、腐败警察、黑手党和迈阿密金钱世界。 含官方音频、视频与英文文稿。
item.content:encoded:
第 505 期 · 2026-11-19

拉里·劳顿结合自身经历谈《GTA 6》与现实犯罪、珠宝抢劫、监狱、腐败警察、黑手党和迈阿密金钱世界。 含官方音频、视频与英文文稿。

本期站方未提供中文精读，以下为英文文稿（早期节目的自动转录存档，可能存在识别错误）。

Lex Fridman (00:00:00): The following is a conversation with Larry Lawton, one of the most notorious and prolific jewelry thieves in US history, who was eventually caught by the FBI, spent more than a decade in prison, including a lot of time in the hole, and then he turned his life around to run the Reality Check program that helps keep at-risk youth out of prison. He now hosts a YouTube channel where he breaks down real crimes, prison life, and how realistic the heists in movies and video games are with, of course, a lot of focus on Grand Theft Auto 3, 4, 5, and now GTA 6. This conversation is in two parts. The first part we recorded just now focused on GTA 6 and some other recent topics. Lex Fridman (00:00:52): The second part we recorded a while back, and it tells the timeless story of his life, the heists, the mob, the prison time, and what it takes to rebuild a life after losing everything. In this conversation and in general, Larry holds nothing back: sex, violence, drugs, robberies, all of it.

He is also, in the time I’ve known him, a truly kind human being, which to me is a humbling glimpse into the complexity of human nature and the paths each of us can take in life and the evolution each of us can go through in life. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here’s Larry Lawton. Lex Fridman (00:01:41): All right. Lex Fridman (00:01:46): For people who don’t know, you were one of the most prolific, notorious jewelry thieves in US history. You were arrested by the FBI, served your time in prison, and since then you’ve done a lot of good for the community helping at-risk youth. And we’ll talk about your life, we’ll talk about your history, we’ll talk about the whole journey in prison, but first we’ve gotta talk about GTA 6. Larry Lawton (00:02:08): I’m an open book, Lex, you know that. And I’m glad to be here. You know, I think you do great work, and I think this is gonna be great- … because you played the game.

Lex Fridman (00:02:17): Yeah, I played in terms of Grand Theft Auto, I played GTA 1, GTA 2, 3, Vice City, 4, and 5. The world that they created is bigger than life. A lot of the things that we love about movies, a lot of the things we love about video games. And I think in terms of GTA 6, in terms of places that are bigger than life, I mean, Miami, South Florida, this is your stomping ground. Like, how does that feel that Grand Theft Auto 6, likely the biggest game of all time by far, is set in this place where you operated as a jewelry thief? Larry Lawton (00:02:54): It’s… I’m going crazy. When I found out, what happened was I- Lex Fridman (00:02:58): You’re basically a GTA 6 character, Larry. Larry Lawton (00:03:01): Yeah. I mean, it’s kinda crazy that way because I didn’t know what GTA was really. I heard of it like everybody else. But I got into it, and it’s really amazing. I got into it so much, I’d lose my head in this game. And then I kept thinking what I would do in this game, what I would do. And that’s what made me start really thinking more about GTA and the game and the crimes, ’cause that’s what I did.

My headquarters was down there in Mia… I started that… Well, my first robbery was in South Florida. It was a setup. But the game, I’m dying to see how they really portray an actual robbery, the actual how much they use for the casing. Larry Lawton (00:03:45): I’ve cased stores for two weeks, and I’ve cased stores for six weeks. You know, I mean, it could take forever to case a store. And I knew everything about a store. And if they wanna do a robbery right, they have to do it from when is the mailman coming, when is packages delivering, when is the sun setting, sun rising, so you could see the glare in the windows. There’s so many variables that go into a robbery. And, you know, being I did so many, probably 25 or more, and, you know, I robbed so many that I had to travel up the East Coast to keep robbing. And I couldn’t rob in New York because of affiliations with organized crime. They’re protected. Larry Lawton (00:04:23): You know, you don’t just go into a store in New York and rob it, especially my day in the ’90s, ’80s and ’90s, because what happened then, it’s protected by the mob. They get protection. And once they find out who did it, there’s no calling the police.

Lex Fridman (00:04:38): And you worked for the mob in New York? Larry Lawton (00:04:41): Yeah, I was associated with the Gambino crime family, and made a lot of money for a lot of people. I had my fence there. I had my people there. I would go in, Lex, with a bag of diamonds worth million dollars, put ’em on a table. When I robbed the jewelry store, I didn’t just rob a little bit. I robbed the whole store. There wasn’t anything left. And it was funny because the government said… You know, I was arrested by a guy named Matt Mullen in FBI. Nice guy, too. I ended up talking to him. He ended up passing away about a year ago, maybe a little more. And he was really good. He goes, “I got you.” You know, he goes, “I was looking for you for six years.” And it’s funny because I didn’t know that, of course. Larry Lawton (00:05:25): I didn’t know that they would flood an area with FBI agents after I did a robbery, the kind of MO I did. And they ended up getting me on great police work. So if anybody says the FBI’s stupid, run from ’em. Don’t walk from ’em, ’cause they’re wrong.

Lex Fridman (00:05:43): So you did a lot of right things to make sure you don’t get caught, and you’re saying they did a good job of figuring it out. Larry Lawton (00:05:50): You know, it took them so long time, six years. And I robbed so many stores. The guy said, “You’re the best I’ve ever seen do it.” And I don’t know if that… I don’t wanna sound like I’m bragging about crime. Larry Lawton (00:06:02): It’s weird, ’cause now I look at that, and I lost a lot of my life. I lost my kids. You know, not good. I have a good relationship with my kids, and my son was just turned seven. He was born November 30th. I got arrested December 2nd, and he turned seven, and my daughter was 15 months old. And my daughter’s in Miami and I see her. My son is in Brooklyn, I see him. No, he now moved to Staten Island. Moved up in the world. That’s what we used to call it back in Brooklyn. You know, you go from the Bronx to Brooklyn to Staten Island or something like that, you’re moving up in the world. And so it’s kinda wild. And now I help people, so I look at it like… I look at robberies all the time.

Larry Lawton (00:06:48): I mean, I can walk down a street to this day, and I don’t care with security cameras and stuff, and I could tell you if I could rob that store, and I could tell you how to do it. And whenever I do, people look and says, “Oh my God, you are 100% right.” And it’s just the little things. It’s people. You’re not robbing technology, you’re robbing people. And when people make mistakes. Lex Fridman (00:07:12): So you’re saying with all the extra technology we have in the world, with all the cameras, with all the surveillance, with all of that, you’re still, it’s still about the people? Larry Lawton (00:07:19): Absolutely. You know as well as I do, technology you can maneuver. You can stop cameras. There’s people who know how to do a lot of that. I’m not even talking about that. I’m talking about people. People are habit driven, so what they’ll do is they’ll go to work in the same way every time, and I’ll know, so I’ll know exactly when they come in, when they come out, who’s there. Even going down to the postal, and you’re going down to deliveries on FedEx or UPS, they come at a certain time in certain areas, and you get to know that.

So I know who’s coming and going in that store, and I know who the neighbor is of that store. Larry Lawton (00:07:56): And I always robbed in strip malls where there’s usually anchored by a big store like a supermarket, like Publix as in South Florida or Winn-Dixie, and they usu- So you could case that store by sitting in a car reading a paper, like your paper, and you’re really watching the store. So it’s a whole different thing when you, when you’re doing it for real. And I’m dying, I really am, wanting to see how Rockstar did it. Lex Fridman (00:08:22): So a big part of it, and you hope to see that in the game, is casing. So doing the research, um- Larry Lawton (00:08:28): Research. What I heard about in the game, now they’re gonna make it where everything is interactive. Like, Jason can make a decision and it goes one way. Lucia can make a decision and go another way. This is what I’m hearing. If that is true, who’s gonna make that decision when… Is it gonna be a, “Oh, he just cased it”? ‘Cause if you just walk into a jewelry store, you’re done. Let’s end the game. Let’s shoot him and get another character, because he’s not gonna make it. He’s gonna be arrested.

There’s no question in my mind. I watch guys think, “Oh, I can rob a jewelry store.” Next thing you know, they write me from prison. Lex Fridman (00:09:00): So what’s the… Casing is understanding all the technology, understanding the, the time of day when certain things happen, understanding the people that are working there, the weak points, the security guards, all that. So all those components. Larry Lawton (00:09:12): Yeah, more, even more than that. It could be where the neighbors are, who’s gonna walk by, when the sun is rising, and when it’s setting so there’s glare on the window. Every aspect beforehand of planning that robbery with things that can make you get caught is part of casing. Lex Fridman (00:09:29): Okay. So what at the biggest level, you’ve seen the extended trailer. We kinda looked at some of it. What do you think they got right? What do you think they got wrong so far? Larry Lawton (00:09:40): I remember some of it. The first thing that struck me right out, right in the opening when he walks up to the place.

When you’re walking up to a place where the… This looks more like a trap house than it looks like a, like a jewelry, a place where they’re doing even… They’re not gonna do something with big money right in a place like this. It’s too scummy, and it’s gonna be decent, where cops aren’t gonna be there every day- Larry Lawton (00:10:03): … ’cause they’re gonna be there, the neighbors are gonna complain, or what are you gonna do? And then when the guy’s security here, guy’s standing there like a gun, like he’s in the Midwest. Like he’s just, gun is in his belt. And they let these two people walk in to a place. They don’t know him. They don’t know if they’re undercover cop. They don’t go with them. First thing I’m looking at saying, “What are they, crazy?” No place on the world, no gangster or no criminal on the planet is gonna let two people just walk through. “Okay, go ahead.” Unless they know you. And it confused me that whole entire trailer because it looked like Jason knew the dog. Larry Lawton (00:10:43): If he didn’t know the dog, that’s a hell of a bad, bad watchdog. And then the guy come in and they’re carrying guns.

They’re all hanging out like they’re doing drugs sitting there. It looks more like a, you would never be manufacturing drugs there and have these kinda characters looking, sitting out front because it’s, that’s a telltale sign. You’re really calling the cops stupid, or on the take. How’s that, even better? And I think that’s gonna be part of it. Lex Fridman (00:11:10): So if he knows the dog, he would probably know a lot of the other people around there. Larry Lawton (00:11:15): Absolutely. And he would even know the area. They, he’s coming in here. He walks in. They let him in right here. And watch what happens with the dog when he walks up. He gets it. First of all, that, he had to get through two people, two, two other people to get to this door. He had to go in. One guy, then he goes to an elevator and another guy stops him. Nobody knows him. No, “Hey, I wanna see somebody.” “Okay.” No. Lex Fridman (00:11:39): How much of this is operating w- where everybody that works there, h- there’s like a circles of trust? How, how much is trust and loyalty and is, is, is crucial to all of this? Larry Lawton (00:11:51): It is supposed to be, number one, about trust.

Obviously, you would not trust this many people. The cops would know this operation is happening. Lex Fridman (00:12:00): Look, look at the ladies in their underwear. Larry Lawton (00:12:02): Well, you know, actually the clothes on that, Lex, is actual normal- … for a house. I knew a bunch. I’ve been in drug houses before. Big drug houses. And what they’ll do is they’ll either be in … scrubs like a doctor’s thing and one set of clothes ’cause you don’t… One, for stealing, but I don’t even worry about stealing. It’s more about don’t have all this stuff all over you when you leave. So- Lex Fridman (00:12:29): Oh, so you can’t steal it or just in general? Larry Lawton (00:12:31): Either both. Either steal it or have it all over you and you’re gonna be pinned out in a minute. Now, obviously, look at amount of people here. There isn’t a chance they would have all these people here. This is another thing. This guy’s putting them on speaker in front of people. That’s not happening. Lex Fridman (00:12:49): There would be more secrecy, you’re saying. It shouldn’t, it wouldn’t be this public.

Larry Lawton (00:12:51): Oh, there’s only… Listen, Lex, I ran a crew, and only certain people knew certain things. Nobody in my crew, nobody knew who my fence was. They mighta knew, but they can- nobody could ever have testified, “Oh, I seen this guy give Larry money.” “Oh, I’ve seen this Larry give him jewelry.” Lex Fridman (00:13:13): Can you explain what a fence is? Larry Lawton (00:13:14): A fence is a middleman. You rob something, you have to give it to somebody who can get rid of it. You have fences who can fence anything, and then in the jewelry… Here’s why people rob diamonds. There was a robbery in France at the Carlton Hotel about, oh, I don’t know, seven years ago, maybe eight years ago. I’m guessing I was on TV on that. And they robbed $140 million in diamonds in a briefcase. You couldn’t carry $140 million in bills. It’s heavy. One of the scenes in here, they’re throwing bags around like it’s like, like not even like weighing Superman. Diamonds, you could pick up 136 mil, whatever it was, and walk out in a briefcase. Now, let’s say you got 20% of that. You know, you’re still talking $25 million. You’re talking about a lot of money. How do you carry $25 million?

Lex Fridman (00:14:15): So these guys the cops found out, so there’s supposedly here crooked cops, right? Larry Lawton (00:14:22): Absolutely, and there are crooked cops. I mean, I dealt with crooked cops. Listen, back in the day, in Miami day, oh, everything was crooked. I used to keep 50,000 in my trunk- … just to, in case I needed it, either to buy something or pay off cops. That’s exactly what you do. They would know it. They go, “What’s in the trunk? Go get it and let me go.” Lex Fridman (00:14:44): So the reality of this world is that there’s some percent of cops that are crooked. Can you speak to… Because there’s a lot of cops who are good. Larry Lawton (00:14:54): Absolutely. I say that as well. Lex Fridman (00:14:56): And that is like they’re essential to the functioning of society, and they’re, I mean, they’re… It’s one of the most, I think, valuable and dangerous jobs is being a police officer, so they deserve respect, I think. But- Larry Lawton (00:15:09): But hold on. I’m gonna go one-on-one with cops ’cause I train cops now. I actually taught the police academy in Missouri, where I’m an honorary cop, which- … that is wild.

I mean, it’s still- Lex Fridman (00:15:20): Yeah, it is. Larry Lawton (00:15:21): I should have brought my badge. I have to give you my badge. And it’s pretty wild. It was very- It was an honor. I mean, it was a big deal. We had 13 police chiefs. They had security. It was newspapers all over the world. And the problem I have with cops is they forget that they’re part of the community and not against it. Talking about regular. You wanna go after these kinda clowns on GTA- … have at it. You wanna mess with regular people for a ticket or be a money grab, which it is, you know, cops stop someone, give ’em a ticket for bullshit. Larry Lawton (00:16:00): And it shouldn’t be. You create this us against them mentality. Now, I support good cops, period. If I was a police officer – honorary I am, but I can’t stop people – but if I had to be a police officer in today’s world, I would be part of the community, not against it. Lex Fridman (00:16:18): You would be a human being. So part of the community- Larry Lawton (00:16:21): First. Lex Fridman (00:16:21): … and if you see a friend, you would behave like a human being first.

Larry Lawton (00:16:25): You know, I had an incident that happened, and I have- I get a lot of this ’cause I help people. Parent called a, you know, had a neighbor who was a cop, said, “Hey, my son’s having problems. Can you talk to him?” and stuff. The kid found- The guy found some paraphernalia, cocaine paraphernalia, whatever it was. You know, he arrested the kid. Come on. You’re trying to help this kid. Do we really need to put a record on somebody? Are we that cut and dry? Are we that non-human anymore? I think- … we have to have feelings, we have to have a heart, and we have to have common sense. We have way too many laws on the books, and we should just get back to common sense. Lex Fridman (00:17:05): Can you speak a little more to that, the fact that there’s crooked cops? What does that just tell you about human nature and about the role of money in society? Larry Lawton (00:17:14): When I was in the game, there was a lot of cops who were crooked, and I’ll tell you what I think that was, though. They were watching a lot of guys make tons of money. And they’re putting their lives on the line making… Okay, even if they made decent money, but it’s not what we were making.

And they got… said, “Wait, what’s the big deal?” ‘Cause I say this all the time. What they pay cops, if I was out there and I’m out in the middle of US 27, which is out west in Florida, it’s in Florida. It’s a very deserted area, and it’s just east of the Everglades. Larry Lawton (00:17:50): And if I’m on 27 and I stop somebody and he’s a drug dealer, and I open the trunk and he’s got, you know, $200,000 in cash and some cocaine in that trunk, I might slam that trunk closed and take that money and say, “Go on your way.” He doesn’t know who I am. I don’t know who he is. Goodbye. Now people are gonna say, “Well, hey, but now you’re one of them.” You know what? I think we’re all together anyway. Just because that guy’s a criminal- does not make him a bad man. I dealt with the biggest drug dealer in the world. I knew Willy Falcon. I was in prison with Willy Falcon. Sal Magluta and Willy Falcon were the two biggest drug dealers in the world. They were Cubans out in South Florida in the heyday. Willy ended up getting convicted.

Larry Lawton (00:18:33): I was in prison in USP Atlanta with him, and he ended up getting a guy… It was really something, Lex, ’cause he paid $5 million for a juror. It’s in the news. You can… I’m sure you can look it up. Lex Fridman (00:18:47): Going to Perplexity here. Willy Falcon, born Augusto Guillermo Falcon, is a Cuban-born former cocaine trafficker best known for running a major Miami smuggling organization with his partner- Larry Lawton (00:19:00): Sal Magluta. Lex Fridman (00:19:01): … His public persona, Falcon, was also a champion speedboat racer during the 1980s. Jesus Christ. This is another GTA character. Okay, you are- Larry Lawton (00:19:10): Oh, 100. I’m telling you. You want GTA to be real? Be where it’s at. Miami was built on drug money. People don’t know that. I was in prison with Willy, and I’ll tell you what a nice guy he was. I used to walk the track with him. And you know, I used to walk the track with him, and I did legal work, so I know a lot of them. Nicky Scarfo, who’s the head of the Philly mob. Vicious. Vicious. He used to walk the track with me, and I’d read his… He’d say, “What do you think of my case?” And I’m thinking, “He’s crazy.

He thinks he’s gonna get out?” “He killed how many people? 30? I don’t know if he’s getting out,” you know? Lex Fridman (00:19:49): When you say walk the track, you’re talking about walking the track in prison? Larry Lawton (00:19:51): Yes, yes. Lex Fridman (00:19:52): Walking around with him talking and- Larry Lawton (00:19:53): Yeah, we’d… You know, when you go for a walk and talk in the track, you know, it’s like two guys will go walk. You know, they’re talking about something. Don’t bother them. It’s like the streets almost, but- … you know, and I was in with all the big guys. W- uh, Vic Orena. Lex Fridman (00:20:06): So you had some heart-to-heart conversations with those- Larry Lawton (00:20:08): Oh, many, many. Not some, many. And you know what, Lex? What I found out, and I mean this, is yes, people, myself included, there’s a good side to these people. Now, don’t get me wrong. I was in prison with psychopaths, and I tell this often. There’s about 200… When I was in Atlanta, we had 880 people who had life sentences. Think, that’s letters. In the federal system, there’s no parole. That means you are never getting out until you’re dead.

They call it life like that, and that literally means that. I had a date, so it was like you had to watch that as well ’cause, you know, people can get jealous. But there were about 200 of those 880 that were psychopaths. Larry Lawton (00:20:56): 200 fight their case legally. They’re always in the law library. They’re working. They’re doing… 400, 500, whatever it is, they find a lover. They literally live together. They go to work at UNICOR. They… I’ve seen punks, they tattoo their blush on them, so they tattoo eyebrows, tattoo their lips red. Make panties with Kool-Aid, dye Kool-Aid for pink panty. I’ve been to weddings in prison. I actually gave 10 books of stamps, that’s money to somebody. So it’s pretty wild, and- Lex Fridman (00:21:28): So romance is still alive in prison. Larry Lawton (00:21:30): … it’s everywhere. Lex Fridman (00:21:31): But that line between good and evil, you know, that’s interesting. You… And I think you made a comment like that when watching the GTA extended trailer. Something about there’s no good guys or bad guys here. So can you talk a little bit more about that line, like there’s good and bad in a lot of these folks?

Larry Lawton (00:21:52): You know, I don’t judge anybody in life. Anybody. I try to help people. That’s my goal now. And the reason I don’t judge anybody because who am I to judge someone? ‘Cause I don’t know what their past was like. I didn’t walk in their shoes. I watched guys who couldn’t read, but are smartest guys I’ve ever met. I always tell people I’m no smarter… I’m no smarter or dumber than anybody, but I’ve been to a place you don’t wanna go, and I could tell you about that place. You know, it’s like, do you wanna hear about what’s gonna happen if you make a bad choice from me or from some professor who read about it in a book? I’m gonna go to the best at what they do. ‘Course that’s what they do. Lex Fridman (00:22:35): And sometimes the dark places life can take you, those have the most wisdom to gain. So people who’ve gone through the dark places, through the struggle, they can teach you the most. Larry Lawton (00:22:46): And survived. Lex Fridman (00:22:47): And survived, yeah. Larry Lawton (00:22:48): Absolutely. I believe it. Lex Fridman (00:22:49): Haven’t been broken by it, yeah. Lex Fridman (00:22:53): You said Miami was built on drug money.

That reminds me of Sam Houser, who’s the legendary co-creator of Rockstar. His brother Dan, Dan Houser, also a legend, brilliant guy, kind human being. I had a podcast with him. Anyways, Sam said a while back when they released Vice City, that was 1980s Miami. He said, “To me, it’s still hands down the grooviest era of crime because it didn’t even feel like it was crime.” Do you agree with him? So you caught the tail end of that era. It was like the peak. Larry Lawton (00:23:25): I was in the late ’80s and ’90s, yeah, early ’90s. That’s my heyday. So absolutely. You know, I had… I had a… Tell you a funny story because I built a clubhouse, like clubhouse or headquarters. It was in a warehouse district. Now, the place was all gangsters. There was a car dealership, car… not… car repair place. Those guys were from the Cleveland mob. Anyway, in this area, I opened a pizzeria. Had money, mob stuff. It was really a headquarters down there. I ended up burning it- Lex Fridman (00:23:59): So it wasn’t an actual- Larry Lawton (00:24:00): Oh, oh, I had great pizza. I love pizza, Lex. That’s my favorite food. Oh, come on. Lex Fridman (00:24:06): New York’s got the best pizza or what?

Connecticut? What? Larry Lawton (00:24:09): Nah, New York. You know- No, not Connecticut. Who said Connecticut? Who brought up Connecticut? That’s got, that’s an insult. Lex Fridman (00:24:17): No disrespect. Larry Lawton (00:24:17): No, that’s, you got insults. Lex Fridman (00:24:18): No disrespect. All right. Larry Lawton (00:24:19): Nah, it’s gotta be Brooklyn. Brooklyn. Lex Fridman (00:24:22): All right. You had a pizza joint in South Florida. Larry Lawton (00:24:25): It becomes the head… You know, I was doing hot diamonds. That’s how, you know, the hot diamonds out of that. Guy- Lex Fridman (00:24:30): What’s hot diamond? What do you mean by that? Larry Lawton (00:24:31): A guy had, was robbing diamonds, and he come to me, and I had the fences. Lex Fridman (00:24:35): It was, like, the center of the operation where the stolen diamonds get converted to money. Larry Lawton (00:24:41): Yes, but him, not mine. Not when I started robbing. When I got to the big time was when my boss said, “Hey, listen, we got somebody who wants his place robbed down there. What are we gonna do? Ba-bum.” It’s gotta be legit. They gotta look legit. But I knew everything. I knew where the diamonds were.

I knew how many people are gonna be in the store, and I still did little cases. Then I said, “Wait a minute. There’s a lot of money in here.” I made 150K back then. Wow, that’s a lot of money. So there is ways to fix, besides the laws, there’s ways to literally take a prison and stop the violence, stop the abuse, ’cause usually it’s a small percentage of the guards that are abusive. You know, and they get power, and they don’t belong in the position to begin with.

You know, it’s the bullying complex kind of thing. Lex Fridman (03:06:35): And they can do a lot of damage. Just one guard can do a lot of damage. Larry Lawton (03:06:38): Oh my God. And even the other guards, just like cops. I do a policing program where what I do. Cops are the same way. I mean, they, you know what- Lex Fridman (03:06:47): They protect each other, you mean? Larry Lawton (03:06:50): Put it this way. People say to me, “Well, Larry, it’s not all of them.” I said, “Let me ask you a question. If I owned a company and I have 100 employees, do I know who the screw-ups are?” I’ll eventually know who they are, and they’re fired. You don’t think out of those 100 guards, all those other people don’t know who the slacker is, who the guy who’s abusing people, who’s got a bad attitude, who’s beating people. You don’t think they know? They know. Larry Lawton (03:07:12): But do you think they’re gonna do anything about it? Here’s why they don’t do anything. One guard saved my life. He was a big Black guy. I wish I knew his name. I’d buy him a vacation. I was in the hole when I was going crazy, and I did things in that hole from flood it.

I got beaten so much that I think I felt alive to be beaten. And he used to come to my cell, open the flat door at night. He worked at midnight the midnight shift. He would open that chute door. He would talk to me through the chute and say, you know… We’d talk about God. We’d talk about life. We’d talk about a lot of things. And he kinda put me in a better mindset for the next upcoming whatever. And he doesn’t know it, but those little talks literally saved my life from going crazy. Larry Lawton (03:08:02): And the compassion he had, you know, and I used to get mad, Lex. I used to get mad. “Why you know this is going on? You’re telling me at night. Why don’t you do something?” It took me until I got out of prison to realize that man is trying to raise a family, feed his own family. He can’t put himself in danger in that place because it is a violent place, and if he don’t get the backing from his guard, something can happen or he can be put on. So it took me, the mature, mature part of me to realize, “Wait a minute. He’s doing that, and he’s doing what he can instead of just, ‘Ah, fuck Lon.' ” Lex Fridman (03:08:40): Like you said, you’re beaten, essentially tortured.

What gave you strength through that, mental strength? Larry Lawton (03:08:48): What made me survive more than anything was I had two young kids, and I just wanted to get out and see them. You know, I really feel there’s so much to do. I love to help people. And now you gotta remember, I got out of prison at 46 years old. I went away at 34, 46. So now I get a phone call, talking to people, doing good, having fun, meeting friends again, you know, starting to adapt a little bit to society. I get a phone call from lady named Jean Bandish. She says, “Mr. Lawton, Judge Rymann would like to see you.” “I ain’t seeing no judge.” She goes, “No, she just wants to hear about certain things.” And I go, “Listen, do you have a warrant? Do you have a subpoena? ‘Cause I’m not coming to see no judge. I know the law.” So, “No,” she goes, “I think you don’t understand. Larry Lawton (03:09:38): She wants to hear this. She heard you talk about kids.” Still scared, thinking, what am I doing wrong? What do they want me for? I don’t trust the system. And I agreed to do it, and I don’t even know how to do anything. So I had my nephew help me, who’s since passed. A nephew helped me with a PowerPoint.

What’s a Power- I didn’t know what a PowerPoint at the time was. So we make 10 slides, Lex, about a PowerPoint. And as we’re doing the PowerPoint, just slides of what I talk to the kids about. I go in on a Friday. I go into the judge’s chambers. Now, we find out years later I’m not even supposed to be back there. I’m on paper and everything. Supposed to have security with me and all that kind of stuff. Now I go to dinner with judges. A lot of them are my friends. Larry Lawton (03:10:26): So we sit in there, I walk in and there’s two other pe- four before them, me, I’m sitting there and, “Oh, hey, Mr. Lawton, how you doing? Thank you for coming. Can you show us what you do?” You know, they helped me put the projector. I didn’t know anything how to do that. I put it in the thing. I had a laptop and put the projector. I tell them what I do. “Thank you, Mr. Lawton. Would you like to stay for the rest of the meeting?” “No. I’m outta here.” And I literally wanna get outta there. You know, I felt ba- I mean, you know, it’s a weird feeling. I do that. I leave. It’s a Friday. Monday morning I get a phone call from Jean Bandish who says, “Hey, Mr. Lawton, I have to give you a heads up.

Judge Rymann sentenced two people to your program.” What fucking program? Larry Lawton (03:11:11): I don’t have a program. From there, I developed the program now. We have a 90% success rate in keeping kids out of jail. We have a 70% success rate by changed attitudes from the parents. We have a 43% success rate in increased education, better grades, and a 31% increase in attendance. And I didn’t do that survey. Eastern Florida State College did that. They asked for the data and people, and they did all the calling. They have a whole thing, graphs, all that stuff. And you would know about that. Larry Lawton (03:11:55): Anyway, they do this data and I ended up getting recognized on the floor of Congress for helping police agencies, ’cause I also have a program where I help integrate police and stop the us against them mentality police have with, police and the communities have. You know, it’s such an us against them. So the program I developed, I was doing myself and doing… And now it’s gotten so big that we had to put it on video and now kids get sentenced with the program.

They have to complete the thing, then they have to take a test and survey that they watched everything, get a certificate of completion, and give it to the court. It’s so powerful. Larry Lawton (03:12:34): If we had that program in Fort Lauderdale right here where Cruz killed the kids from the high school, and I lived right near, not far from that high school they woulda had, the police woulda had a tool to try to intervene and help this kid before he went crazy because, you know, they had many interactions with that kid and they never gave him a… They didn’t have anything. Even if it didn’t work, they could say they tried. We tried this program or that program. We gave it to him. We tried to help the parent and, I mean, police have a tough enough job obviously and to pick something out, but when you have that many interactions with somebody. And we even put it where it can be used for detention. Larry Lawton (03:13:17): Kid does something stupid in school, he has to go there, he has to watch the program, he has to pass the program. And then you could see, ’cause I do a whole survey and I could show you thousands and you could see the mindset.

And if you saw a kid that said, you know, “I hate the world anyway. I might as well just shoot someone,” boy, red flag can go off. You can then get counseling into this kid, find out really where his head’s at. There’s ways to do things, again, with young people and mostly because they respect me. I’m not one of the system. Mm-hmm. I wouldn’t rat, so my credibility is right. I’m not a former drug addict, so it’s not, “Ah, I’m not gonna do drugs. He was just a drug addict and cleaned his life out.” Everybody wants to make money. Larry Lawton (03:13:59): Everybody wants to be somebody. And then so you take all those positives and you bring them to a kid and I have video reviews from kids that make me cry ’cause they, you know, some of them have rough lives and when you hear how they this one kid, man, it’s so powerful, starts crying on my… I mean, I want to hug the… I did actually. And he’s young, maybe 19, 20. ‘Cause we found out my program is not just for teenagers. It’s for kids 25. Kids we all know, and you’ll know this, a young man’s brain doesn’t mature till 25, a female about 23. Not my numbers, psychology numbers, and it’s true.

So and you know, anybody making bad choices needs a wake-up call what could happen to them if they keep making bad choices. Larry Lawton (03:14:49): And then that program actually works with cards with police agencies, so they actually carry a video card. The card is actually the video. It’s like a credit card. It’s got a QR code with a code for the police. The police chief opens the message. Says, “We’d like you to watch this video. It might help your child in a trial.” The kids watch it and they- the police chief closes it by saying, “We hope this helped you. If you have any problems, please contact us.” Each cop carries them, 10 of them in their pocket. Larry Lawton (03:15:18): And, you know, we’re gonna push more of that. That’s where the government loved- I mean, I used to work with the Weed and Seed program. That’s a government agency which, again, funding. They take the funding away. Weed and Seed program was a program that the government gave, and they would go to a neighborhood and weed out the bad with the US attorney. This is federal now. They’d take the US attorney in that area.

They’d get the drugs off the streets, get the gangs out of there, and then seed it with programs like mine. Larry Lawton (03:15:50): So it was Weed and Seed program. It was a very successful program. Again, funding cut that, which drives me crazy when you have a program like that with success rate. And I used to go speak at the things, and my program was vetted by the federal government, and they used it. And then I spoke in Texas, actually. In Texas, they have the International Association of Police Chiefs headquarters, and I’ve spoke there to the executive board, actually because there’s one of my mentors in the policing who gave me a badge. And that’s weird, ’cause I’m not a supporter of most police. Most police who are screw-ups don’t deserve- And I’m not gonna lose my reputation ’cause some jerk-off police chief wants to make me, you know, think he’s great. No. Larry Lawton (03:16:36): There’s a police department in St. Louis, in Lake St. Louis unbelievable. A guy named Mike Force. To this day we’re friends. He’s retired. Now to Nucci, I’m still an honored police there. I got the car. It all works. Maybe get me out of a ticket. I don’t know. I don’t even use it.

I don’t even carry it. But they’re so positive- Larry Lawton (03:16:55): … ’cause they really think about how to help people, and their first thing is not arrest. It’s help. He says, “Anybody starts telling you arrest, they don’t understand the game.” It’s, “How can we help you?” You know, when I teach police academies, and I did in St. Louis, is the first thing a cop should do when they pull somebody over is not say license or registration. How about going up to the guy and saying, “Excuse me, sir, are you okay? You know, you ran that stop sign, and I’m not even gonna give you a ticket. I just wanna make sure you’re all right, because people get hit broadside, and a lot of people can get killed. Are you all right? Everything good?” “Yes, I’m…” “All right.” And what community positive. Larry Lawton (03:17:39): That guy goes home, tells everybody in the world how cool the cop is instead of, “License and registration. You know what you did? You blew the sign.” Who the fuck are you, kid? You know, especially as a 22-year-old cop, and I’m a 60-year-old man. I wanna strangle him.

And then you have a battery to that, but they have to understand they’re part of a community, not just us against them. We’re the cops. We got the gun. Lex Fridman (03:18:03): And those stories travel. The good and the bad stories travel, so you gotta put your good- Larry Lawton (03:18:07): You- Lex Fridman (03:18:07): The good ones out there. Larry Lawton (03:18:08): … 100%. And, you know, you get enough- And that, that all happened because a friend of mine was 78, since passed, but 78, and he gets stopped. He had four people in the car going to dinner. He rolled a stop sign, and a cop comes up. “You rolled it.” He told the story to everybody I know. “You rolled it.” “What?” “License. You rolled the sign. Give me your license.” Then he came back and threw the… He said, “I can’t give you a ticket ’cause I got a call, but don’t roll it.” He told that story to every person I know, and instead of, “Sir, everything all right?” Elderly man, nice, very successful guy, just stupid. Lex Fridman (03:18:51): What advice would you give to young people? Larry Lawton (03:18:57): Make sure your word is good. That’s probably the number one thing, I think. I think- And, and it starts early.

If you say something, do it. And that doesn’t mean you can’t have a mistake, and people will know you have mistakes. Own up to them. Don’t think life’s over. You know, I also tell people this, and this I think is very important. A lot of young people come up to me at 30 years old and say, “Ah, I can’t do it. I can’t make it. I, you know, I messed up.” I said, “Hold on, buddy. I was 46 years old with a record that you don’t have, and I had to get out of prison and start over. How do I do it? Perseverance, work hard, don’t give up.” You know, the people who give up either are looking for pity. I don’t believe in pity. I believe in working hard. Larry Lawton (03:19:49): I think people who do work hard will get a hand up by a lot of people, ’cause people like to see that. And that, to me, is the biggest. Your life’s never- And I mean that for older people. Again, 46 years old, you’re getting out of prison. Life’s not over. Find out what you love to- I love what I do. I- As you can tell. I do. I mean, I love people, and I love to talk to young people. But, you know, Nick working with me, and his energy matches mine, and that’s pretty tough. I mean, I just have a lot of energy.

Listen, when it’s all over, the lights are out, I’ll have plenty of time to rest. You know? Lex Fridman (03:20:27): I agree. So make sure your word is good and then work your ass off. Larry Lawton (03:20:32): And never quit. Lex Fridman (03:20:33): Never quit. Larry, you’re an incredible human being. Larry Lawton (03:20:37): Thank you for having me. I really appreciate that, you know? And thank you- Lex Fridman (03:20:40): You better be a character in a Grand Theft Auto game. I’ll put my vote in. Thank you, Larry. Larry Lawton (03:20:45): Thank you very much. Lex Fridman (03:20:47): Thanks for listening to this conversation with Larry Lawton. To support this podcast, please check out our sponsors in the description, where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. Thank you for listening, and hope to see you next time.

中文精读网页版：https://lex.qiaomu.ai/ep/larry-lawton/

item.title: #504 俄乌战争：普京、泽连斯基、无人机与战争的未来
item.description: 围绕俄乌战场上的无人机运用、双方领导人与战争走向，讨论现代战争形态的演变。
item.content:encoded:
俄乌战争与无人机 · 第 504 期 · 2026-11-10

围绕俄乌战场上的无人机运用、双方领导人与战争走向，讨论现代战争形态的演变。

俄军一天要放飞 8000 到 10000 架 FPV 无人机。这只是单向攻击用的穿越机，还不算侦察机、光纤机和其它战术型号。一个月下来，几十万架。

Michael Kauffman 是卡内基国际和平基金会高级研究员，主持 War on the Rocks 平台上的《Russia Contingency》播客。他在 Lex Fridman 播客第 504 期里给出这个数字，顺手补了一句：这些消耗品的数量，已经远远超过战场上人员和装备的总数。

按常理推，仗打到这个份上，应该是无人化的、屏幕后的、按按钮的。事实正好相反。每一架 FPV 后面都坐着人，往往还不止一个。

一个典型的无人机小组需要两到三个人。一个飞手，一个副手兼导航。这是极其消耗精力的工作，你得整天盯着屏幕飞。还得有人当技术员，负责装弹药、排查故障。（Michael Kauffman）

所以这场被外界称为"第一次无人机战争"的冲突，本质上是一场人力密集的战争。只是人力从战壕挪到了屏幕前，从扛枪变成了扛电池。

2026 年的错位：地面上最好的一年，城市里最难的一个冬天

先把这个时间点的基本盘摆清楚。战争进入第五年，两位嘉宾给出的判断有一个共同的结构：战场上和战场外，方向相反。

Michael 的说法是，2026 年是乌克兰自 2023 年夏季反攻以来地面作战表现最好的一年。同一时间，俄罗斯的成绩是 2023 年冬天以来最差的一年。他甚至给出了拐点：2025 年夏天，俄军的打法开始出现明显的边际收益递减。

更具体一点，乌克兰今年若干次局部进攻行动拿下的土地，比 2023 年那场被寄予厚望、准备了几个月的大反攻还要多。那场反攻失败了，今年这些没人提前宣传的小规模行动反而成了。

另一边，俄罗斯把重心压到了战略轰炸上。从 2022 年秋天开始，俄军就用巡航导弹加短程弹道导弹打乌克兰的电力设施、变电站、供热厂。到 2026 年，打击清单已经扩展到仓库、数据中心、学校、医疗设施、商场、火车。Michael 提到最近几个月有好几座购物中心被击中。

打击手段本身也换了代。早期靠巡航导弹和弹道导弹，现在主要靠大量单向攻击无人机做饱和突防。这些无人机从廉价的螺旋桨型号，进化到喷气动力，本质上已经是轻量级的地面发射巡航导弹。

战略轰炸在历史上从来没有好成绩，尤其是当地面战役失败或者陷入泥潭的时候。但几乎每一位政治领导人都会觉得，这一招对自己可能管用。（Michael Kauffman）

这就构成了 2026 年的核心错位：乌克兰在前线占优，后方的城市却在承受开战以来最密集的打击。前线的优势和后方的脆弱同时存在，谁也抵消不了谁。这个冬天有多冷、电网能撑多久，直接决定谈判桌上谁说话更硬。

战线在哪里

Preston Stewart 是西点军校毕业、在阿富汗服过役的老兵，现在做 YouTube 频道、播客和《Defense Tech News》简报。他把地理讲得很清楚。

主战场仍然在东部和东南部。基辅位于国土中部，不面临俄军步兵和短程无人机的直接攻击，但每天都在承受远程无人机和导弹。往北走，苏梅和哈尔科夫有俄军的越境渗透，规模不大，目的是建立缓冲带。

再往南就是顿巴斯，卢甘斯克和顿涅茨克。整场战争最血腥的战斗都发生在这里。乌克兰把这一带修成了所谓"堡垒带"，从莱曼一路延伸到斯拉维扬斯克、克拉马托尔斯克、德鲁日基夫卡、康斯坦丁尼夫卡。前线士兵嫌康斯坦丁尼夫卡名字太长，直接叫它 Konstaha。再往西是多布罗皮利亚，目前是乌军防御的锚点，它后面还有一串城市。

扎波罗热是个特殊区域，双方同时进攻。俄军试图从胡利亚波莱往西推，而东北方向，乌克兰一支空中突击旅组成的战术集群整年都在做"蠕动式"进攻，一点点往前啃。莱曼方向，乌克兰第三军打了一次代号"维瓦尔第"的进攻行动，收回了 2025 年丢掉的地盘。

所以"阵地战僵局"这个说法并不准确，至少在战术层面不准确。Michael 反复强调，2026 年的战场流动性比 2024、2025 年高得多，双方阵地犬牙交错，中间是一大片灰色地带。

灰色地带是什么样子

传统理解里，防线是一条线。这里不是。乌克兰很少维持连贯的防御线，更多是三个人一组的哨点，彼此间隔几百米。四公里范围内可能只有三个这样的点。

为什么这么稀？前沿太容易被无人机发现和打击，兵力一密集就是活靶子。真正的前沿是点状的、带大量空隙的。空隙靠什么补？靠无人机巡逻覆盖所有接近路线。

这套体系的有效半径，Michael 估计是前线前后各约 15 公里，各地不同。越过这条线的东西，无论人还是车，被发现就意味着被追杀。这个区域，前线士兵管它叫 kill zone，杀伤区。

俄军的应对方式是渗透。集中装甲集群往前推这套已经不干了，因为那种集群在 10 到 30 公里外就会被远程无人机盯上，还没到前线就被消耗掉。现在改成小股步兵，或者摩托车、全地形车，甚至拉达轿车。

这是不计人命才成立的战术。你可以一点点啃地形，最后总能啃下来，代价是路上损失 90% 到 95% 的人。（Preston Stewart 引述一名在乌军服役的美国海军陆战队志愿者）

算一笔账就明白了。派十个人上去，七个没到，三个到了，并且找到了乌军哨点之间的缝隙。后方指挥官立刻知道这条路径是通的，下一批十个人就沿着这条路送。三次之后，乌军防线后面可能已经有七八个俄军在活动。再往后三五公里，就是乌军无人机小组的位置，那些人正在飞 Mavic，手上没有步兵武器，根本没准备接敌。

这就是渗透的真实机制。目的在往后渗，正面突破从来不在考虑之内。威胁补给线，逼迫乌军的无人机操作员和后勤往后撤。他们一撤，前沿的覆盖就稀了，更多俄军就能进来。循环往复，地图每次只动一点点。

击毁一辆坦克，需要多少架无人机

外界看到的视频几乎全是命中集锦。这造成了一个严重的认知偏差：一架几百美元的 FPV 飞过去，一辆几百万美元的坦克就炸了。

Michael 给出的实际数字完全是另一个量级。击杀一名步兵，平均需要大约五架。击毁一辆步兵战车，15 到 20 架。击毁一辆坦克，通常 30 到 40 架。他见过一段未公开的视频，7 月在野外，用了 12 架才解决一个人。

极端案例是 79 架。那辆俄军坦克加了全套电子战设备，外面焊了一圈像谷仓一样的防护棚，属于最高防护等级。

还有一个数字更能说明饱和程度：一个机械化连发起进攻，现在预期要承受接近 300 次命中，也就是说，绝大部分车辆是被打中好几次之后才报废的。

视频有强烈的锚定效应，而且所有视频都是成功的。没有失败集锦。除非你在现场收集数据，否则你根本不知道命中率是多少。（Michael Kauffman）

把这几组数字放在一起，会得到一个反直觉的结论：这套打法的核心变量是数量。精度在这里早就不是瓶颈，供给才是。战争没有变便宜，只是把一枚导弹的钱换成了三十架塑料飞机加三十个操作员。

一根 50 公里的光纤

整场访谈里最不符合直觉的技术细节，是光纤制导无人机。

电子战干扰是无人机最大的敌人。常规对付办法就是压制信号，让无人机在某个区域失效。俄罗斯在库尔斯克战役期间率先大规模使用了一种解法：在无人机屁股后面拖一根极细的光纤，直接连到操作员手上。信号走线不走空，干扰器全部失效。

那个东西就是一个线轴，跟钓鱼竿上的绕线轮一模一样，光纤细得像鱼线。你飞的时候得小心，得慢，要想着线怎么绕过树、怎么铺在路上。（Michael Kauffman）

代价是载荷变小、航程受限、操作变笨。收益是彻底免疫干扰，而且极难被探测。

Preston 讲了一个细节。乌军车上普遍装一种叫 Chuika 的探测器，三根天线，能接收三个频段的模拟图传信号。当敌方无人机离你比离操作员更近时，你车上的屏幕会直接显示出那架无人机的视角画面，你等于在看敌人的摄像头。这在战场上已经是标配。而光纤无人机不发射任何信号，Chuika 上什么都不会出现，直到炸弹落下。

射程目前已经推到约 50 公里。这个数字第一次听到时确实难以消化：一根 50 公里长的线，绕在线轴上，跟着一架自杀式无人机飞出去。

光纤机的占比目前还不高，Michael 估计在 15% 以下。但它改变的是战场感知的对称性，因为看不见的威胁比看得见的威胁更消耗士气。

2022 年 2 月：所有人都算错的那道题

回到开头。Michael 承认，他在 2021 年就判断俄罗斯会发动全面入侵，而且判断对了规模。他错的是方式。

我们把俄军的行动过度理性化了。没有把他们的军事计划和俄罗斯的政治假设绑在一起看。（Michael Kauffman）

俄罗斯的政治假设是什么？情报部门已经铺好了路，乌军会迅速崩溃，俄军会被当作解放者迎接。他们可以打一场斩首行动，快速突进，包围基辅，抓捕或隔离乌克兰领导层。抵抗即使出现也是短暂的，之后直接进入维稳占领阶段。

这套假设的源头，是普京根本不认为乌克兰是一个有独立民族认同的国家。2021 年 7 月他写过一篇文章，把这些观点白纸黑字写了下来。分析界看到了那篇文章，却没有把它当成作战计划的输入变量。

另一重误判在乌军身上。Michael 说得很坦白：

我们绝大多数专业积累都是针对对手军队的。对盟友和伙伴的军队，我们的了解少得多，这是这个行当的天然局限。（Michael Kauffman）

结果就是，关于俄军进攻计划的情报，比关于乌军防御计划的情报多得多。信息的丰富程度本身就成了判断的锚。

他还提了一个更大的方法论问题：军事力量不能被抽象比较。说美国第一、中国第二、俄罗斯第四，这种排名没有意义。军事力量必须放在具体情境里才有意义，地理、政治目标、作战构想，这些决定了部队怎么用，而怎么用才是决定性因素。

Preston 补充的角度是军事文化。开战头几周，俄军有数量惊人的高级军官阵亡，原因是他们不得不亲自往前线跑，去疏通堵在路上的车队。为什么？因为下级没有决策权。整个系统在等上面的命令，上面不来，路就堵着。

乌军和北约体系相反。任务式指挥，指挥官意图往下传，具体怎么打由最基层决定。Preston 在阿富汗见过 20 岁的上士做可能决定全组生死的决定。这套东西被北约教官带进乌军，在 2022 年 2 月发挥了作用。

没有命令的时候，他们仍然知道任务是什么，仍然能做出当下最好的判断。这是我们从第一天就看到的差别，到今天还在。（Preston Stewart）

巴赫穆特：一座小城如何变成政治符号

2022 年 8 月到 2023 年 5 月，围绕这座城市打了十个月。Michael 讲得很细，因为它几乎是理解这场战争的模板。

巴赫穆特本身地形不利，城市在低处，东西两侧都是高地。俄军先占了东侧高地，然后同时打两场仗：一场是城内的逐屋争夺，另一场是城外的包围战，目标是切断补给道路。守方最怕的是后者。

打头阵的是瓦格纳。普里戈任获准从监狱招人，组建囚犯突击队。战术很直接：一批一批送上去消耗乌军，乌军打得累、弹药打光，再上有经验的老兵。俄罗斯空降兵负责掩护两翼和提供炮火支援。等到俄军拿下这座城市时，城里已经没剩什么了。

真正的关键概念是 Michael 提出的"巴赫穆特综合征"：在已经不该守的时候继续守。

每当一座城市被宣布为"堡垒"，我就会担心。因为这意味着守军无法及时撤退。被派进去的乌克兰士兵也这么想，他们知道那会是一场苦战。（Michael Kauffman）

为什么明知不划算还要守？因为 2022 年秋天乌克兰在哈尔科夫和赫尔松连续打出两次成功反攻，势头正好。基辅担心丢掉巴赫穆特会让西方公众和政界认为战争已经转向，进而影响援助。城市本身不重要，重要的是它成了一个信号。

事后看，证据很硬：从巴赫穆特到下一座城恰索夫亚尔，俄军走了一整年。再到拿下恰索夫亚尔大部分地区，又花了一年。丢掉巴赫穆特在军事上远没有当时看起来那么致命。但它确实消耗掉了一批最有经验的部队，这些部队本来可以被轮换下来，用西方装备重新训练，去打 2023 年那场夏季反攻。实际上去打的，是装备更好但没经验的新兵，任务是难度最高的破障作战。

Preston 点出了这个模式的普遍性。现在看康斯坦丁尼夫卡，正在重复同样的形状。什么时候该撤，是个判断问题：在你还能以有利交换比消耗对手的时候守，是合算的；一旦补给线被切断、开始被迫用反击来维持阵地，那就已经过了临界点。这个临界点在实际操作中极难识别，而且政治层面的决定往往压过军事判断。

厨师的兵变，和一支军队的"瓦格纳化"

2023 年 6 月 23 日到 24 日，瓦格纳向莫斯科进军。这是整场战争里少有的、结局完全不可预测的 48 小时。

起因是权力斗争。普里戈任不断公开攻击国防部长绍伊古和总参谋长格拉西莫夫，把瓦格纳包装成比正规军更能打的替代方案。巴赫穆特之后，绍伊古下最后通牒：所有瓦格纳人员必须和国防部签合同。这等于要收编普里戈任的私人武装，断他的根。

他选择了兵变。瓦格纳占领了罗斯托夫，那是俄军在乌克兰作战的总部所在。然后两支纵队沿公路向莫斯科推进，一路击落俄军直升机和固定翼飞机，给空天军造成不小的损失。他们带着坦克、防空系统和步战车，一支货真价实的机械化部队。

我不认为他们接近成功。莫斯科是个巨大的城市，就算进去了也不知道能干什么。他们的目标是用向莫斯科的推进作为谈判筹码，换特赦、换资产交接。（Michael Kauffman）

在高度个人化的威权体制里，替代者会被优先清除。大多数政变在策划阶段就被情报部门掐灭，能真正跑起来的极少。这次跑起来了，恰恰说明体制当时出现了裂缝。但普里戈任没有精英支持，没有替代普京的可能，所以结局是谈判、撤兵、流亡。

2023 年 8 月 23 日，他的私人飞机在特维尔上空爆炸，机上多名瓦格纳高层同时死亡。Michael 的判断没有任何含糊：这是一次公开的处决，用来给其他人看。

故事到这儿还没完。Michael 提出了一个词：瓦格纳化。

瓦格纳这个组织死了，但它某种程度上感染了俄罗斯军队。俄军大规模照搬瓦格纳的战术，组建了 Sturm-Z、Sturm-V 这样的囚犯突击连，把突击群编制铺到各个营和正规部队里。（Michael Kauffman）

后果是双面的。短期内，突击群战术提升了俄军的进攻能力。长期看，俄军过度专业化于小规模突击行动，逐渐丧失了组织和执行更大规模复杂作战的能力。这也是 2025 年之后边际收益递减的原因之一。

普里戈任自己说过，仅巴赫穆特一役瓦格纳就阵亡两万人。而俄军后续在整场战争中使用囚犯的总数，比这多得多。

地图上的谎，要用命去圆

这一段是整场访谈里最具体、也最沉重的部分。

俄军上报的战线，长期比实际控制线靠前 10 到 15 公里。为什么会这样？一个士兵摸到某个村子的地下室，举旗拍个视频，地图上就把这片标成已控制。最近甚至出现了用 AI 生成的假升旗视频，被俄罗斯自己的军事博主骂了回去。

这不光是宣传，它直接损害作战。

他们按照自己并不真正控制的战线去组织火力支援。轮换进场的部队拿到的是错误信息，以为自己的前沿在某个位置，实际那是交火区。结果是自己的士兵被打死。（Michael Kauffman）

更荒诞的连锁反应在后面。谎报持续几个月之后，上级会说：拿出来给我看。于是部队被迫在 10 月到 11 月发动强攻，去真正拿下那些早就报上去的村子。这就是为什么每年这个时段的攻势会突然加剧，伤亡也跟着飙升。

库皮扬斯克是最好的例子。格拉西莫夫向普京汇报说合围了当地所有乌军部队，普京还公开邀请国际记者进去看。Michael 当时就在库皮扬斯克西边，和乌军一个旅的人一起看这条新闻。他说得很克制：这事儿连让人笑一下的门槛都过不了。

后果是实际的。俄军据此认为那个方向不再需要那么多火力支援和空中力量，把资源调走了。前线士兵想呼叫空袭，却因为上报的战线已经变了而叫不到。

为什么会有这种系统性的谎报？Michael 给了三层解释。第一，士兵和军官之间缺乏信任，部队凝聚力差。第二，惩罚型文化，任何错误都要担责，说谎的激励很强。第三，指挥权高度集中，真正有权限的是远离战场的上级，下级只负责执行。信息一旦在源头失真，整个决策链条就是垃圾进垃圾出。

乌克兰也有类似问题，有指挥官因为瞒报被解职。但结构和文化不同，程度轻得多。Michael 也提到乌军指挥官的两难：上级不许撤，丢了就得夺回来，可手上没有兵力夺回来。是拿人命去填一个明知守不住的位置，还是瞒报保住自己的兵。这不是干净的选择题。

两位统帅

Preston 的观察是，泽连斯基把军事决策大幅下放，不插手战役战术层面。这通常是对的。普京在战略层面深度介入，但看起来不太 micromanage 战术执行。2022 年上半年俄军打得很糟的时候，他确实直接联系过集团军群级别的指挥官，那属于战役层面。

真正的差别在信息的质量和目标的现实性。

泽连斯基拿到的图景要真实得多，对乌克兰处境的评估更准确，目标也更现实。普京拿到的不是。（Michael Kauffman）

Michael 的判断很直接：俄罗斯这场战争存在政治目标与可用军事手段之间的根本错配，责任完全在普京。他发动了战争，作为政治领导人，打了四五年还看不见这个错配，就该向自己提一些难回答的问题。

这场战争可以切成两段。前 30 天，从 2022 年 2 月 24 日到 3 月底，是俄罗斯试图斩首基辅、扶植傀儡政权的阶段。这个阶段彻底失败了，而且在当前战争条件下无法重来。乌克兰是不是一个独立国家、有没有独立的民族认同，这个问题在那 30 天里已经有了答案。

之后的一切，是一场消耗战。它决定的是边界在哪里、经济能不能撑住、战略取向是否要做出让步。俄罗斯的谈判要求至今没变：乌克兰承认顿巴斯剩余部分归俄，限制军队规模，限制武器种类，放弃加入北约，限制西方驻军，俄语地位，东正教会地位。这些要求对应的是俄罗斯希望自己达到的战场位置，跟眼下的实况差得很远。

普京最近的说法是，泽连斯基甚至无权讨论扎波罗热、赫尔松、顿涅茨克、卢甘斯克的未来，因为那些是"历史上的俄罗斯土地"。而俄军要拿下这些地方，还得跨过第聂伯河。

钱、人和 2027 年

战争什么时候结束？Michael 给的判据很简洁：当双方都认为谈判的结果好过继续打能拿到的东西。

问题在于俄罗斯的要求没有随战况调整。而支撑战争的资源还在。

经济层面，俄罗斯把 44% 的政府预算投向战争，约占 GDP 的 9% 到 10%。今年春天，俄罗斯关键的经济精英开始公开说这个支出水平不可持续。钱大量流向军事生产，而军事产品在经济上不产生价值，等于经济体在缓慢地吃掉自己。但 Michael 的判断是，俄罗斯有资源打到 2027 年。

人力层面，俄罗斯的人口优势是压倒性的。麻烦在于某些地区已经开始填不满征兵指标，出现了影子动员，也就是变相强制。Preston 说，这正是乌克兰几年前就已经经历过的事，现在轮到俄罗斯，而后果难以预测。

外部支持是另一根支柱。乌克兰没有西方资金、武器和情报支持撑不到今天。俄罗斯这边，中国提供了关键的经济通道、机床和零部件，朝鲜在最紧张的时候供应了俄军约 40% 的炮弹，还派兵参加了库尔斯克作战，伊朗的份额小一些。

美国现在的角色变了。没有直接资金援助，但军售和情报支持仍在，账单由欧洲支付。乌克兰对美国的依赖程度比战争初期低，但在关键领域仍然依赖。

两位嘉宾对美国这一年的处理方式评价不高。Preston 的说法是，美国主动从一个支持乌克兰争取有利结局的联盟领导者，变成了一个自称中立的仲裁者。这个转身同时得罪了两边：欧洲盟友不再信任美国的意图，乌克兰立刻怀疑自己要被出卖。而俄罗斯从来没把美国当中立方看，这一点莫斯科自己都懒得掩饰。

我们放弃了杠杆。当我们还在提供武器的时候，我们在和平进程里有更多的话语权。现在这个杠杆没了。（Preston Stewart）

Michael 的批评更结构化。上一届政府的口号是"需要多久就支持多久"，那是个口号，不是计划。欧洲盟友有好几年时间拿出方案，也没拿出来，共识只有一条：支持乌克兰。今年总算有人逼各方明确自己的停战条件，这件事本身有用。但执行方式是反复无常的，对盟友和乌克兰都不可预测，而且政府内部有一部分人明显想和俄罗斯恢复正常关系，把这场战争视为障碍。

停火之后的那六到八个月

最后回到那个最难的问题：这条路怎么走完。

Michael 的短期判断不乐观。俄罗斯目前把继续打当作优于谈判的选项。普京可能在等两件事：一是这个冬天的打击战役能不能把乌克兰逼到更弱的谈判位置，二是明年春天欧洲的选举，比如法国，会不会产生对俄更有利的局面。

他认为可能出现的，是局部、分隔化的停火。比如双方停止打击能源设施，或者停止攻击黑海航运。这类安排有现实基础，也容易监督。

真正风险在于，停火很容易变成一个重新武装的间歇期。乌克兰几个月后必须复员，前线的人想回家。俄罗斯的部队大部分是合同兵，可以不复员。如果停火之后没有真正的安全保障，六到八个月后乌克兰会极其脆弱。（Michael Kauffman）

这不是假想。2014 年之后有两份明斯克协议，都没能通向政治解决。这场战争的起点本来就是 2014 年。Michael 担心的是第三次：这一场怎么结束，决定了下一场怎么开始。印巴、阿以、亚美尼亚和阿塞拜疆，都是同一场冲突的多次迭代。

再往远看，乌克兰战后的国家存续能力，很大程度上取决于欧洲是否把它当作自身安全的一部分。俄罗斯的问题更难，因为它不是一个人的问题。这是一场失败的帝国转型的产物，苏联解体不只是一个日期，是一个持续的过程，而俄罗斯至今没有变成一个后帝国的欧洲民族国家。Michael 说，他不认为这是命定的，欧洲历史上有很多帝国最终放手了，只是很少是自愿的。

访谈临近结束时，两位嘉宾讲了两个故事。一个是 Skyfall 公司用大型无人机吊着吊舱，飞 30 公里把一名无法撤出的伤员运回来，吊舱里有对讲，一路上有人跟他说话，告诉他还有几分钟，干得好。第二天视频里，那个人坐在医院病床上，孩子坐在腿上。

另一个是 Code 9.2 的一段旧影像。两名伤员被无人地面车后送，途中被俄军无人机击中，车瘫在半路。连长看到画面，开着一辆皮卡冲过去，没穿防弹衣，把两个人一个一个扔上车，全速撤出。

打久了的人，你会发现他们没丢掉人性。幽默、眼神里的笑、彼此之间的爱。战争里最糟和最好的东西，常常出现在同一天。（Michael Kauffman）

给跟踪这场战争的人：几条具体做法

  • 看战况通报时，先找地图来源。俄方公布的战线长期比实际靠前 10 到 15 公里，用俄方地图做判断会系统性高估俄军进展，也会误判某地是否即将被围。
  • 看到无人机击杀视频，在脑子里乘一个系数。击杀单人平均约 5 架，步战车 15 到 20 架，坦克 30 到 40 架，极端情况 79 架。视频只发成功的，命中率被严重高估。
  • 评估某座城市是否该守，看三个信号：补给道路是否被火力控制、守军是否被迫用反击来维持阵地、伤亡交换比是否还对自己有利。三条里出现两条，就已经过了该撤的临界点。
  • 判断停火消息的含金量，别看停火本身，看配套条款。有没有安全担保、双方是否同步复员、监督机制由谁执行。缺这三样，停火大概率只是下一轮的准备期。
  • 对技术的判断，盯住"人力比"而少看"智能程度"。这场战争里绝大多数系统仍然是人在远程操作，一套无人机小组要两三个人。任何声称"全自主"的说法，先问它在总架次里占几个百分点。
  • 如果你在做硬件或机器人产品，把抗干扰当成一等需求。光纤制导无人机之所以有效，唯一原因是它绕开了整个干扰维度。有时候绕开问题比解决问题便宜得多。
  • 判断战争走向，把战线和后方放在同一张图上。前线的优势和电网的脆弱可以同时存在，而谈判筹码往往由后者决定。

英文原稿（Lex Fridman 官方页面）：https://lexfridman.com/ukraine-war-preston-stewart-michael-kofman/
中文精读网页版：https://lex.qiaomu.ai/ep/ukraine-war-preston-stewart-michael-kofman/

item.title: #503 数学中的 AI 危机：纳维-斯托克斯方程、黎曼猜想与复杂性理论
item.description: 探讨 AI 对数学研究构成的危机，涉及纳维-斯托克斯方程、黎曼猜想与复杂性理论等核心难题。 含官方音频、视频与英文文稿。
item.content:encoded:
第 503 期 · 2026-10-26

探讨 AI 对数学研究构成的危机，涉及纳维-斯托克斯方程、黎曼猜想与复杂性理论等核心难题。 含官方音频、视频与英文文稿。

本期站方未提供中文精读，以下为英文文稿（早期节目的自动转录存档，可能存在识别错误）。

Lex Fridman (00:00:00): All right, so this is a kind of emergency episode, I think it’s fair to say, about the state of mathematics and artificial intelligence. A kind of crisis moment in the history of mathematics. Over the last few weeks, machines claimed to have solved some of the hardest problems in the history of math: Navier-Stokes, the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, the unique games conjecture, and hundreds of other results. So here with me, we have Steven Brunton, who’s a mathematician, fluid dynamics expert at University of Washington, who can speak to Navier-Stokes, turbulence, all things fluid, and many other topics. Lex Fridman (00:00:43): Also, here’s Ankur Moitra, a mathematician and theoretical computer scientist at MIT, visiting Institute for Advanced Studies in Princeton this year, who can speak to many things: unique games conjecture and complexity theory in general, and the mathematics of how the AI learns, and all things theoretical computer science.

And Alex, a mathematician, number theorist at Rutgers, who can speak to also very many topics, including Riemann hypothesis and Lean, the automated proof and the automated verifier and checking and so on, and so many other topics in mathematics. All three are brilliant. Lex Fridman (00:01:27): All are very kind to show up this early morning and talk to me, assemble this kinda multi-agent mini swarm of human brains to try to interpret what happened in this very moment. Lex Fridman (00:01:56): A lot of mathematicians, brilliant mathematicians, including Terence Tao and others, are freaking out. It’s a mix of awe, terror, dread, and few inklings of light, of hope also. So I apologize to start with a question about feeling, but what have you been feeling about this historic moment? Maybe Alex, do you wanna go first? Alex Kontorovich (00:02:08): Yeah, I don’t know if I would call it a crisis. There’s a lot of opportunity in that crisis. It’s a, it’s a chance to rethink what it is we’re trying to accomplish, and it’s the chaos of opportunity that some people are reacting negatively to, some people are reacting positively to, and sometimes those reactions are happening in the same person.

And so I think we’re entering, if we’re not already in, a period of some kind of golden age of mathematical knowledge after millennia of having a candle that we are walking around the woods, and this is as far as we can see. Now we have a flashlight. Lex Fridman (00:02:46): I think we should comment on the magnitude of this moment for people who are not aware. So maybe to quote you, something like “Holy shit, if a human did this, it’d be an instant Fields Medal.” Maybe you didn’t say, “Holy shit,” but basically saying this is an incredible result. So a lot of people wouldn’t have expected this amount of progress in this amount of time, so this is truly shocking. So you’re now speaking as a person who is dealing with the feelings you’ve felt over the last couple of days, having found this out. So maybe also it’d be useful to go back to the feeling you were having when you first saw the report that, in this case, OpenAI dropped. Lex Fridman (00:03:27): And the two of you happened to be on camera loosely on the same day, maybe a few drinks in because it was a conference or a get-together. Maybe, Ankur, you– can you speak to what you were feeling?

Ankur Moitra (00:03:40): It was an interesting night when the results dropped. Now, it was not entirely unexpected because for weeks there’d been rumors about the two biggest problems in my areas that were in that collection of results, so the unique games conjecture and RL equals L. There were even rumors about matrix multiplication, so really my first reaction was, “Wow, it’s all true. Thank goodness it’s finally out there because now people can actually go through it and process what’s happened and figure out what to do next.” Now, as to your earlier question, you know, what are we feeling? Well, for me, it changes on a daily basis, but I think the biggest, most overarching feeling is really feeling like you’re getting pulled in two very different directions. Ankur Moitra (00:04:24): My work has always been about asking the right questions, and to that extent, these tools are amazing for me because, you know, they increase my ability to learn about other fields. It’s like having a world expert who’s there to teach you about things in your own language. Your ability to make connections is just magnified.

But, you know, one of the parts of my job that I really love the most is the mentorship aspect. Not just training grad students and postdocs and seeing them do great things, but having them come with me on these journeys. So the part that pulls me in the other direction is the recognition that, you know, the playbook and the blueprint for success that we had for so long is now thrown out the window. Ankur Moitra (00:05:07): So it becomes a lot harder to advise students and postdocs about, you know, what are things they should be working on that are gonna make an impact, are gonna make a name for themselves. So I feel very excited, but maybe more intellectually lonely than I felt before in part because, you know, a lot of times great results come from asking very humble questions, at least for me. And now there’s so much anxiety and dread and feeling that, wow, you would have to do something really momentous to stand out in the sea of AI results, that it feels like we’ve lost some of that patience in terms of planting the seeds from which the great oak trees grow.

Lex Fridman (00:05:49): Terence Tao, Fields Medal winner, wrote, “I am horrified by the many person-years of ongoing patient and deliberately slow research efforts, particularly by graduate students and postdocs, toward many motivating problems in mathematics being casually disrupted or destroyed by such a release.” Much as one cannot unhear a movie spoiler or a crossword clue, one cannot explore a problem as profitably and richly once one is aware of an existing solution, and I mourn the path not taken and the opportunities lost in the frantic race to develop the technology. So I mean, if we’re being realistic, it’s more dramatic for a PhD student and a postdoc than maybe the way you’ve articulated. Lex Fridman (00:06:38): I mean, you’re saying it quite calmly, but if I was a PhD student right now, I’d be in a state of, like, shock. Like, my whole life– I was going through some of this. I know a lot of my friends are programmers. They’re going through this state of shock in last December when basically most of the programming world switched to AI writing most of the programs. So I would approximate it to a feeling of kind of a loss of meaning, kind of terror, like dark stuff.

We’ll keep exploring that. Steve, what do you think? What were you– what are you feeling? Steven Brunton (00:07:15): I would say most of my feelings are pretty hopeful. I think I’m an engineer. I like solving, you know, problems that make technology more realistic for humans, artificial hearts and airplanes. And our ability to solve real applied problems is going to get much, much better. Our scope and reach is gonna increase, and so for that, I’m extremely hopeful. But there is a lot of uncertainty, and I think, you know, some of this fear of meaning, of losing control, of you know, just being kind of cut out of the process that we all love being a part of it is a little scary. Steven Brunton (00:07:55): And I don’t think any of us would be surprised at either of the kind of two paths that might take place over the next five or 10 years, where we really are just dwarfed by you know, other intelligence, or it kind of levels off, and this becomes an incredible tool that we use for our curiosity, for our human problem-solving. And that uncertainty is massive. Those are two very different worlds. And so uncertainty is difficult for humans.

I think it’s also difficult for those of us who have chosen math. We chose math, you know, probably because we liked rules and formalism and, you know, uncertainty is uncomfortable. I think the humility aspect is really important, though. This is a really good opportunity for us to remember why we’re doing this. Steven Brunton (00:08:44): Like, what is human purpose? It’s not to be famous. It’s not to have a Fields Medal. You know, solving interesting problems, helping other people, being curious, just wanting to understand the world—those are really good things to kind of get back. Like, what do we need to be satisfied humans? And I think that’s a really interesting moment for us to think about. Like, I’ve been thinking about it a lot lately. It is more difficult for young people, right? Like figuring out how to find their way. But I actually have more faith in them than us in a sense. Lex Fridman (00:09:19): Do you think there’s something to what Terry says about it’s harder to be motivated when you know a problem has been solved, to explore that space when a problem’s been solved like this by an AI system?

Steven Brunton (00:09:36): Yes and no, in the sense that I do very much agree that the path is as important as the destination. Like, if you go on a road trip, the road trip is, you know, is usually just as fun as, as getting there. At the same time, if we found out that another country had invented teleportation or time travel, I guarantee we would reinvent it in the next five years. Like, if you knew it was possible and you could reverse engineer a little bit, we would be curious, we would dive into it, and we would figure it out. So knowing there’s a solution also is an incredible motivation to get there much faster. Lex Fridman (00:10:14): Let me ask the question this way. If this moment marks the moment of the trajectory where AI basically, quote-unquote, “solves math” or kills math, can you make the case that that is in fact a trajectory, and then can you make the case that that is not a trajectory? Can you steelman both paths?

That this is a path towards which, like, mathematics as we know it is done completely, so that’s gonna be a thing done by machines, and then what humans do is something fundamentally different, or there still will be something that looks similar to our current mathematics. Can you steelman both cases? Alex. Alex Kontorovich (00:11:02): Yeah. So, you know, you said two things, and I’d like to separate them. One is solve math, and the other is destroy math. So, uh- … let’s make that precise. What does solve math mean? If you think back to when chess engines first came out and people were like, “Oh, this is gonna be amazing. We’ll play centaur games.” So this is a human being plus a computer system against another human being and a computer system, and that lasted like 10 seconds- … and then the computers got so good that if you did anything but choose the top move that the computer recommended, you would lose. Alex Kontorovich (00:11:33): And so the human being’s role in that game became, “Yes, accept the first move. Yes, accept the first move.” That’s no longer fun, and we don’t see many games of centaur chess anymore, right?

And so in fact, I just had a conversation with a colleague named Thomas Goberta where we axiomatized our argument for what the future might look like, and one of the axioms that I’m willing to even accept for the sake of argument is what I call the solved axiom. And the solved axiom says, let’s assume at some future point, we’re nowhere near there now, and I don’t expect us to be there necessarily. We’ll see, you know, where the capabilities taper off if they do. Alex Kontorovich (00:12:14): But let’s assume the solved axiom, which says any mathematical problem that can be solved with human interacting with AI could also have been solved by AI alone. That’s the solved axiom. So that would mean that really there’s nothing new for a human being to cont– you know, you can say to an AI system, “Okay, I have problem X, I wanna think about problem X,” but the only way that I will make progress, any progress that it’ll make on problem X, will just be press a button. The AI thinks about it. It doesn’t necessarily solve it, doesn’t mean that it’ll solve every problem. The Riemann hypothesis is not solved, okay? That’s what I really want the solution to.

I just didn’t think in my lifetime I would see any kind of progress- Alex Kontorovich (00:12:55): … towards it that we saw a few days ago. So it’s not that AI systems are solving every problem. They’re solving every problem that could be solved by humans interacting with AI. That’s what that axiom would be. So I’m saying, if we are ever in that world, does that necessarily destroy mathematics? And my strong argument is no, I don’t think it destroys mathematics. Lex Fridman (00:13:18): If that axiom is true, what’s the role of humans? Alex Kontorovich (00:13:21): So I don’t think that mathematics, pure mathematics, not engineering mathematics, not things that will cure cancer and, and solve, you know, jet– everybody has a jet pack or whatever other technological advancement you might imagine. Pure mathematics, you know, we know that we’re proving theorems just because we’re curious about them. I don’t think the solution to theorems living in ones and zeros in data centers is valuable to human beings. I think the value of pure mathematics is that it lives in the heads of human beings.

Ankur Moitra (00:13:52): So just to, you know, add to this, I mean, I’m glad you came right out with the question that’s on everyone’s minds. So thank you for that. I would caution against overfitting to one objective function for this, right? Ankur Moitra (00:14:04): Because, you know, we used to think of ourselves as just the smartest things around. You know, human mathematicians can solve, you know, reach the highest treetops. But now we’re faced with the fact that many of the problems that we thought were, you know, quite a ways out have been solved by AI. But maybe one of the consolations we can take is actually the fact that we’re very computationally limited compared to the way that AI is solving it. You know, given the same finish line of proving the same theorem, I can’t really hold that many papers or ideas in my head at one time. Ankur Moitra (00:14:36): So in order for me to reach that same finish line, maybe I have to develop more generalizable and abstractable ways of getting there that then help you not just solve that one problem, but, you know, explain connections or other directions you want to get into, right?

So it’s always amazing when you look back on papers you’ve written, and you can see these threads, invisible sometimes, that connect different areas of work, because developing systems of ways of understanding problems helps you for surrounding problems, not just to get a lean, formalized, you know, one theorem down. Lex Fridman (00:15:11): But the interesting thing here is those threads, what you’re saying is sometimes invisible, are quite visible to the AI systems now. It seems like that’s perhaps the actual very reason why they’re able to make so much progress, is they can extract the threads and pull on them because they have the view of the so many papers. Ankur Moitra (00:15:31): I think it depends on what you mean by threads. You know, for me, the reason you prove results is so that you better understand the world around you. Mathematics, to me, is a vehicle for abstraction and understanding things. And you know, it’s when you have a major result, what’s important is not just the truth of the statement, but what you’ve learned en route to doing that. Usually, people’s first question is, “Okay, you proved something fantastic, but how did you do it?”

And then people, once they digest that new idea, that new definition, that new way of looking at things, there are lots of other problems nearby that fall. So somehow you’re building structures that help you attack not just one problem, but a whole sea of problems. Ankur Moitra (00:16:15): And, you know, it’s not that we need fully formalized, you know, results to do that. Sometimes we reason in very sloppy metaphors that, you know, help us conceptualize the world around us. Lex Fridman (00:16:27): And how much of this is something Alex mentioned offline, attention is all you need. How much of this is the human ability to shine a light on particular areas that, quote-unquote, matter? So the human ability to ask the right questions, the important questions. Alex Kontorovich (00:16:42): That’s always been the case. So within this– before AI, there’s a– you can think of, like, here’s the axioms, and just abstractly from the axioms, you can get to logical deductions, right? There are theorems that we could prove from the axioms. And there’s a much, much, much larger space of theorems that we could prove than the space that human beings ever actually care about.

And so, you know, so by, almost by definition, it’s like a tautology that the theorems that we’ll get excited about are the theorems that we care about as humans. So maybe AI can convince us that there’s some interesting structure. Maybe it can say, “Hey, look over here. Let me give you this new definition or something.” It hasn’t done that yet. Lex Fridman (00:17:19): And sometimes the mechanism by which we select the things that we care about, it could have an application. So Navier-Stokes is connected to fluids and all natural systems. But it could also be a thing that some kinda mixture of beauty and difficulty that just pulls at us. Maybe there’s an intuition. You know, the prime numbers are full of these really complicated problems that maybe don’t have an obvious application in the immediate sense, but it pulls at us somehow. And maybe as a symptom of the pursuit of the hard thing, great applied mathematics and engineering and solutions to real world problems comes out. Ankur Moitra (00:18:06): So just, you know, as an example, right?

A lot of times when I’m working on a problem, I might have some, like, bigger goal that I want to accomplish, but usually what I do is I try to find the simplest, most embarrassing open problem that I still don’t know how to solve. You know, that aspect of like digesting it down to something, boy, how can we not know this? It, you know, it feels like it’s on the right track because then when we can solve that example, maybe we’re assembling the set of tools we need to make attacks on other problems. So I do think we’re gonna have to become a lot more deliberate about, you know, what do we care about? How do we use these tools from a metacognition standpoint? You know, what exactly are we delegating to them and what are we not delegating to them? Ankur Moitra (00:18:49): And we’re really at the beginning stages where we’re just trying to piece it together as we go along. You know, on the one hand, looking for a proof is kind of like exploring this tree of possibilities. You might have some intuitions based on some other proofs you’ve seen about, you know, which directions to go in. Maybe I should go down this branch, maybe I should go down this branch.

But sometimes we encounter, you know, points on the tree which have really high branching factor. We just don’t know which way to go down. We don’t even have a guess about if we went down them, what would we discover? And now in this centaur world of math, we suddenly, you know, have something else intelligent that we can interact with, right? Ankur Moitra (00:19:28): And what is the right way to use that tool to search for the beautiful theories, I think will be challenging and evolving, but it’s important to not lose sight of the fact that we don’t just care about theorems. So I, you know, I’m a mathematician, I’m a theoretical computer scientist, but I’ve also been reading a little bit more broadly, you know, about social sciences just to sort of make my peace with all of the changes that have been happening. One of the things that really stuck in my mind that I liked is there’s something called the doorman fallacy, which is very interesting. So the idea is that you take a complex job and you boil it down to its simplest, most visible task. So what does a doorman do? I guess they hold the door for people as they’re coming and going, right?

Ankur Moitra (00:20:12): And when we lived in New York, we really enjoyed talking to our doorman. You know, they were wonderful people, but, you know, if you digest it down to just that simple job, you can think, “Oh, I can replace them just by a sliding door that detects when people are going or coming,” and you miss out on all the aspects of their job that, you know, add a lot of value and are harder to articulate. And I think that’s a good way to think about mathematics in the age of AI too. What does a mathematician do? You know, the simplest and most visible part of the job is we prove theorems. And, you know, theorems about conjectures that were open for hundreds of years, like Fermat’s Last Theorem, these are very visible things that we’ve spent a lot of time popularizing. Ankur Moitra (00:20:57): But I don’t think that that’s all that a mathematician does. I like to think about it as a mathematician is someone who thinks deeply, and a byproduct of thinking deeply is, you know, proving old conjectures, but it’s also building new theories, building new ways of looking at old things, making new conceptual connections.

And these are parts that you know, maybe AI will swallow up too, but we’re not there yet at this moment. So even though this is a momentous time, I don’t think it’s the right time to hit the panic button. Ankur Moitra (00:21:27): I think it’s the right time to really recenter in terms of what our values are and have these conversations as a field, and remember that what we do really has a plurality of different aesthetics and goals, and that when one thing becomes cheap, like problem-solving for well-defined things, it makes the other things that are orthogonal to it all that much more valuable. Lex Fridman (00:21:49): That’s actually really beautiful. The doorman fallacy, going to Perplexity here, is the mistake of reducing a person’s job to its most obvious task and assuming that automating that task replaces the value of the whole role. A hotel decides, quote, “We’re paying someone to open a door. An automatic door can do that more cheaply.” But in fact, the doorman also welcomes guests and recognizes returning customers, handles luggage and hails taxis, provides security and discourages unwanted visitors, and signals prestige and makes guests feel cared for.

Ankur Moitra (00:22:23): That was my favorite part. I looked up what a doorman does, and boy, we have a lot of commonalities with mathematicians. If I don’t signal brand value, I don’t know what I’m doing. Lex Fridman (00:22:32): Exactly. That’s funny. But I think the task for us humans in general, but also mathematicians, is to come up with that list, like actually make more explicit exactly what it is that humans do. And I haven’t heard any of you mention beauty. I apologize if I’ve mentioned beauty excessively already. But there’s something that mathematicians are, from my outsider sort of fan perspective, are kinda expositors, scholars of things beautiful, broadly defined. Alex Kontorovich (00:23:08): That’s exactly right is until five seconds ago, there was a near perfect correlation between the ability to solve new deep theorems and what we actually want as human mathematicians. And what we want is exactly what you said, beauty and understanding and depth of thought, and the fact that you can press a button and get what used to be our proxy without any effort, without any deep thought, and without any necessarily knowledge.

Like we have people saying, you know, “Do a breakthrough,” and then putting whatever they find on Twitter and now, you know, what are mathematicians supposed to do with that? Steven Brunton (00:23:48): I would go one step behind answering questions and doing problem-solving is asking the right questions. So like that is how I think you measure good problem-solving is asking the right sub-questions, asking, you know, a question that is interesting and can be solved and can be interpreted. And so I feel like the value of asking good questions is– has always been something we value in our colleagues, and that’s gonna become increasingly more valuable. Ankur Moitra (00:24:16): I agree completely, and just to, you know, emphasize a point that was sort of hidden in there, I think asking the right questions requires a lot of mathematical insight. Alex Kontorovich (00:24:26): Mm-hmm. Absolutely. Ankur Moitra (00:24:26): So, you know, you’ll see people make that comment all the time, you know, “What are we gonna value going forward? It’s asking the right question. It’s giving great talks.”

But, you know, I wouldn’t minimize, not that you were, but just to be explicit, I would not minimize the role in mathematical insight in both of those tasks, because it’s when we say that, you know, talks will become more important, I’m not imagining that, you know, we’re all gonna become Twitter influencers- and TikTok whatevers. Alex Kontorovich (00:24:53): I hope not. Ankur Moitra (00:24:54): I hope not. Because, you know, really what stands out is having ideas that get adopted by your community that end up becoming powerful over time. So, you know, I wanna tie this back to something that Lex brought up earlier on, which is, you know, he asked, am I being overly optimistic? Probably, right, compared to you know, how grad students view these things. But I think one of the things that I’m most worried about in the near term is what’s gonna happen to our systems and institutions. You know, it’s not just hiring and tenure and all these things, but it’s really that when a grad student starts off their PhD, you know, they’re a new entrant to the field.

Ankur Moitra (00:25:32): They’re trying to absorb what are the techniques in their field, what are the important problems, and they’re trying to figure out how to make a name for themselves. And what we used to do is we would give them a blueprint that was very simple to follow. Take a problem people care about and improve it, and then people will know who you are. You know, you’ll get papers in top venues. You know, doors will open for you. But now I think that blueprint has changed in a lot of ways because there are so many results that are happening right now that we’re all just overloaded with it, and I think it’s okay to take time to rethink that blueprint.
